title: The Varna Verse
hook: one verse names four groups from one body. it has been used to rank people by birth, and fought over ever since
carry: one body, and careful hands for a hard verse
tomorrow: where did the moon come from?

segments.voice: Yesterday, God fills the world and is still more. Then the great offering: spring as butter, summer as fuel, autumn as the offering, and from it creatures, chants and verses.

When they divided the Purusha, into how many parts did they arrange him? What was his mouth? What were his arms? What are his thighs and feet called? That's the Purusha Sukta's eleventh verse, in paraphrase, nothing but questions, like a teacher quizzing a class. The answer comes in the next verse. It's short, and it has been recited, defended and fought over. You met the caste question on day ninety-five, and in the Gita on day two hundred twenty-two. Today, the verse itself.
screen: `WHAT WAS HIS MOUTH? HIS ARMS?` → `A VERSE OF QUESTIONS.` → `AN ANSWER THAT'S BEEN FOUGHT OVER.`

segments.voice: Verse twelve answers, in paraphrase: the brahmin, the priest, was his mouth. His arms were made the rajanya, the ruler and warrior. His thighs became the vaishya, the people of trade and farming. From his feet the shudra, the laborer, was born. Four groups, from one body. Notice the wording. The verse doesn't use the word varna, the later word for these social orders, and it doesn't say higher or lower. But readers have heard a ranking in mouth and feet, and that's where the argument begins. Some traditional readers take the verse as the sacred origin of the four varnas. Over time it was also used to defend a ladder fixed by birth, and people outside the four orders altogether were treated as untouchable. Reformers, among them B. R. Ambedkar, attacked that use of the verse directly and fought the system it was used to defend. Other readers, Hindu teachers among them, stress that all four come from one body, and point to the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna says the four orders were made according to qualities and actions, arguing birth was never meant to decide them. These readings don't agree, and this path won't pretend they do. India's constitution abolished untouchability in 1950, and many Hindus today reject any ranking by birth. If a friend asks you about caste, you can say what the text says, what people did with it, and who was hurt. A verse can be held sacred and still need careful hands.
screen: `MOUTH, ARMS, THIGHS, FEET.` · `ONE BODY. THE WORD VARNA ISN'T THERE.` · `A LADDER BY BIRTH, AND ITS CRITICS.` · `QUALITIES AND ACTIONS, NOT BIRTH?`

segments.voice: Give each part of the body the same few breaths: the mouth, lips and tongue resting; the arms and hands; the thighs, their weight on the chair; and the feet, which carry everything and are usually noticed least. No part gets more; if you pray, you can pray for anyone who has been treated as less.
The Purusha Sukta. In its twelfth verse, mouth, arms, thighs and feet become four groups of people, and readers have argued over what that means ever since.
Your line: one body, and careful hands for a hard verse. Say what it says, and who was hurt. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindus read the Purusha Sukta's verse on the four groups in sharply different ways: some as the origin of the varnas, others as a picture of one interdependent body, and reformers have challenged its use to justify caste by birth.

notes: SENSITIVE DAY: the varna verse. The script states the text, then three readings without ranking them: the traditional origin of the varnas; its use to defend caste by birth and untouchability, with Ambedkar's critique; and readings stressing one body and the Gita's qualities-and-actions line. A Keeper, and ideally a Dalit scholar, should check balance and wording.

Historical claims not in the cited text: 'over time the verse was also used to defend a ladder fixed by birth, and people outside the four orders were treated as untouchable'; 'reformers, among them B. R. Ambedkar, attacked that use of the verse directly and fought the system'. Ambedkar's critique is in Who Were the Shudras? Confirm wording.
Text claims to confirm: 10.90.12 reads brāhmaṇo 'sya mukham āsīd bāhū rājanyaḥ kṛtaḥ, ūrū tad asya yad vaiśyaḥ padbhyāṃ śūdro ajāyata; the word varṇa does not appear; rājanya, not kṣatriya, is used.
Glosses: vaishya as 'trade and farming', shudra as 'laborer'; confirm they are fair and not demeaning.

'Some point to the Bhagavad Gita' (4.13, cātur-varṇyaṃ mayā sṛṣṭaṃ guṇa-karma-vibhāgaśaḥ): paraphrased; the Gita uses the word varna there. Confirm the reading 'birth was never meant to decide them' is fairly attributed to some readers, not to the Gita itself.
The hook says the verse has been fought over 'in temples and in politics'; general, confirm or soften.
Editor: cut the speculative 'in ways the poet could hardly have pictured' and the unsourced 'in temples and in politics'; 'holy' framed as 'held sacred' so the narrator does not assert it.
